title: Steak and grilled foods
why: Protein and fat soften tannin. Char and a full red often enjoy each other.
alt: A cooler Pinot Noir if the grill is about mushrooms and vegetables more than a thick steak. Sparkling water with lime if you are not drinking.
avoid: A delicate, sweet white will taste thin beside a charred steak. It is not wrong. It is just outvoiced.

title: Seafood
why: Acid and a clean finish let fish taste like fish. Cream and oak want a richer match.
try: Sauvignon Blanc, a crisp Chardonnay, or dry sparkling wine with shellfish. A lighter Pinot Noir can work with salmon.
alt: Unoaked white if the fish is simply grilled. A richer Chardonnay if there is butter sauce. Iced tea is not the move. Cold sparkling water is.
avoid: A big tannic red with oysters. The metal note some people taste is real enough to skip.

title: Pasta and tomato-based dishes
why: Tomato is acidic. A wine with its own acidity meets it instead of tasting sour or flat.
try: Sangiovese, a brighter Zinfandel, or a dry rosé.
alt: If the sauce is creamy rather than tomato, look at the creamy-dish card instead. A chilled herbal soda or lemon water keeps the same brightness without wine.
avoid: A very oaky, low-acid white. The tomato will make it taste tired.

title: Creamy dishes
why: Richness wants either bright acid to cut it, or a wine with enough body to stand beside it.
try: A richer Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc, or Champagne. Acid is doing the work, not butter in the wine.
alt: A light red with good acidity, such as Pinot Noir, if the dish has mushrooms. Sparkling water cuts cream too, without competing.
avoid: A tannic Cabernet with a cream sauce. The tannin can taste bitter when fat and acid are not balanced.

title: Cheese boards
why: Fat softens tannin. Salt makes fruit taste sweeter. Strong cheese needs a wine that will not disappear.
try: Firm sheep cheese with Tempranillo. Goat cheese with Sauvignon Blanc. Blue cheese with a sweet fortified wine, if you want that classic.
alt: One wine for the mild cheeses and water between the strong ones. You do not need a different bottle for every wedge.
avoid: Assuming a single red works with every cheese. A fresh mozzarella and an aged blue are not the same problem.

title: Pizza
why: Tomato, salt, char, and melted cheese are a crowd. A wine with acidity and not too much oak keeps up.
try: Sangiovese, Zinfandel, or a dry rosé. Sparkling wine is a quietly excellent pizza wine.
alt: A cold lager is outside this app’s job, but a citrus soda or sparkling water with the same salt and acid idea will not embarrass the slice.
avoid: A delicate, expensive bottle you are saving for a quieter night. Pizza is joy. It is also loud.

title: Vegetarian dishes
why: Vegetables have bitterness, sweetness, and char of their own. Match the preparation, not a rule about meat.
try: Sauvignon Blanc or dry Riesling with herbs and greens. Pinot Noir or Sangiovese with roasted mushrooms and tomato. Grilled vegetables can take a Syrah.
alt: If the plate is spicy, look at the spicy-food card. A good nonalcoholic bitter soda can play the same refreshing role as a high-acid white.
avoid: Choosing a huge red only because dinner feels important. Importance is not tannin.

title: Mushrooms and earthy flavors
why: Earthy food likes earthy or savory wine, and it also likes a little acidity so the dish does not taste muddy.
try: Pinot Noir, Sangiovese, or an older, less oaky Tempranillo. A mushroom risotto can also like a richer Chardonnay.
alt: If the mushrooms are grilled and smoky, Syrah joins the conversation. Black tea is a sober echo of tannin, if you want one.
avoid: A very sweet wine. Earth and sugar rarely shake hands.

title: Spicy food
why: Heat makes alcohol taste hotter and tannin feel harsher. A little sweetness, or lively acidity and low alcohol, keeps the peace.
try: Riesling with a touch of sweetness, Gewürztraminer, or a chilled dry rosé. Sparkling wine can work if the dish is salty more than fiery.
alt: If you want no alcohol, a cold lassi, sweet iced tea, or sparkling water with citrus will calm heat better than a big red.
avoid: High-alcohol Zinfandel or a tannic Cabernet with a very hot dish. The wine will shout back.

title: Desserts
why: The wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert. Otherwise the wine tastes sour and thin.
try: A sweet Riesling or Chenin with fruit tarts. Port or another sweet fortified wine with chocolate or blue cheese. Not every dessert wants Port.
alt: A ripe pear and a cup of tea is a complete ending. You can also stop before dessert. The meal does not require a last glass.
avoid: A dry red with a sweet cake. The cake will make the wine taste bitter.
